newsitem.title: UK: U.S. rate worries markets, Euro-bourses fall.
newsitem.headline: U.S. rate worries markets, Euro-bourses fall.

text.p: Major European bourses fell sharply on Monday -- a trend mirrored on Wall Street -- as worries about credit tightening weighed on markets ahead of an important U.S. interest rate meeting on Tuesday.

On Wall Street, the Dow Jones Industrial Average tumbled more than three quarters of a percent or about 50 points within minutes of opening as investors worried that an increase in interest rates could take a bite out of the U.S. economy, hurting 1997 earnings.

"It's getting sloppy out there. The light volume says you should attach a little less importance it ... but there's no question that people are worried," said First Albany chief investment officer Hugh Johnson.
Leading London stocks were down over one percent, or about 40 points, shortly after Wall Street opened. Declining shares were in an eight-to-one majority but volume was light.
On Friday, the blue chip FTSE 100 index closed down 10 points after hitting an intraday peak of 3,994.1 -- just short of the psychologically-important 4,000 level.
The rate-setting meeting of the U.S. Federal Open Markets Committee on Tuesday was overshadowing both stock and currency markets.
"People will just be sitting tight, desperately keen to keep out of trouble," said one trader.
In Frankfurt, German shares ended bourse trade down nearly one percent, slipping on profit-taking after recent sharp gains and on uncertainity ahead of Tuesday's Fed rate decision.
The 30-share DAX ended bourse trade down 19.06 points at 2,627.04.

And on the Paris bourse shares also fell further from opening losses on profit-taking, with dealers cautious about U.S. rates and because of book-squaring on the last day of the September accounting period.
Dealers said the firming of the franc against the mark was not helping shares.

Peugeot fell 1.7 percent to 572 francs after it said its profit for the first six months of 1996 shrank by more than half as a brutal price war in France took a heavy toll on the domestic car industry.
On the currency markets, the dollar was steady, with trading volumes low in the absence of Tokyo overnight, which was closed for a holiday.
However, the mark lost ground against European currencies, particularly the French franc, following the weekend European finance ministers' meeting in Dublin.
The gathering pace of Europe's drive towards monetary union, not only put pressure on the mark but also lifted the European currency unit to 21-month high.
On Friday the mark slipped to a two-month low against the franc. It weakened further to a 3-1/2 month low early on Monday to around 3.3810 francs before recovering somewhat.

"Having ridden on the crest of a wave of optimism about EMU prospects, foreign exchange markets will shift their attention back to monetary policy this week, with the key event clearly being the FOMC meeting on Tuesday," said Klaus Baader, currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
The markets were counting on quarter percent U.S. rate rise and only a surprise half-point increase would shake the dollar out of its well-trodden ranges, analysts said.
On the precious metals market, platinum fixed at the lowest level for nearly 2-1/2 years as weakness in silver pressured the rest of the precious metals complex.
Platinum fixed at $386.50 per ounce, the lowest since April 20, 1994, compared with $387.25 on Friday afternoon.
Heavy selling by US investment funds and other speculators last week shaved 13 cents off the price of spot silver, pushing it below the key $5.00 per ounce level.
CURRENCIES AT 1400 GMT
The dollar was at 1.5145 marks and 109.85 yen compared with 1.5141 marks and 109.76 yen in Europe late on Friday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1400 GMT
The Financial Times-Stock Exchange index of 100 leading British shares had fallen 39.2 points to 3,924.9.
In Paris, the CAC-40 share index dropped 11.47 to 2,067.99.
The 30-share DAX index in Frankfurt closed down 19.06 at 2,627.04. PRECIOUS METALS
Gold was easier was at $381.20 compared with a close of $381.75 in London on Friday. Silver fixed at $4.88 cents.
